question: Can the known compositional architecture of a neural network be used to derive a first-order optimizer whose step magnitude, width/depth scaling, and schedule are set automatically rather than tuned as learning-rate hyperparameters?

key_findings.claim: The paper introduces functional expansion, an exact decomposition of a composite objective's linearization error into model-linearization and loss Bregman-divergence terms, then sets the former term to zero by assumption.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 1 is an algebraic identity for any differentiable model and loss. Assumption 1 declares the dataset-averaged inner product between the loss gradient and nonlinear model remainder to be exactly zero for the chosen update; under that equality, Theorem 1 rewrites the perturbed objective as its first-order Taylor term plus the output-space Bregman divergence. This is a conditional expansion, not a general majorizer for nonconvex composite models.

anchors.section: A proofs of Proposition 1 and Lemmas 1-2

key_findings.claim: For a bias-free fully connected ReLU network with square loss, AGD normalizes each layer gradient, scales it by width and 1/depth, and computes a scalar step from the current average gradient magnitude.
key_findings.evidence: Prescription 1 fixes input, target, weight-operator-norm, and update-operator-norm scales. Deep relative trust bounds the output perturbation by sqrt(d_L)(exp(eta)-1). Under Assumptions 1-2, Theorem 2 minimizes the resulting bound with eta = log((1+sqrt(1+4G))/2) and Delta W_k proportional to -sqrt(d_k/d_{k-1}) grad_k/(L ||grad_k||_F).

anchors.section: A proofs of Lemma 5 and Theorem 2

key_findings.claim: The claim of a rigorous hyperparameter-free optimizer rests on two exact, unverified structural assumptions that are especially restrictive for the implemented minibatch setting.
key_findings.evidence: Assumption 1 depends on the selected finite update and sets a nonlinear remainder inner product exactly to zero. Assumption 2 requires every layer gradient to have stable rank exactly one, even though the paper notes that a batch gradient is a sum of rank-one matrices and could have stable rank up to the minimum of layer dimensions and batch size. Neither assumption is measured in any experiment or enforced by the code.

key_findings.claim: The critical-point and global-minimum rates do not establish convergence of the released experimental algorithm.
key_findings.evidence: Lemma 8 proves min_t G_t^2 <= 11/T only for full-batch square-loss FCNs under Assumptions 1-2 and the exact dimensional prescription at every step. Theorem 3 adds a deep Polyak-Lojasiewicz lower bound with unspecified alpha to obtain L(w_T) <= 6/(alpha^2 T). Experiments instead use stochastic minibatches, allow prescribed weight norms to drift, add convolution, residual connections and batch normalization, and use cross-entropy on ImageNet.

key_findings.claim: The cross-entropy route used for ImageNet is heuristic rather than the claimed analogous majorize-minimize derivation.
key_findings.evidence: Lemma 2 identifies the output-space Bregman divergence with a KL divergence, but bounds it only through a local second-order expression containing an uncontrolled O(Delta f^3) remainder. Corollary 2 calls this a majorization, then assumes the output perturbation is 'reasonably spread out' so its infinity norm behaves like its Euclidean norm divided by output dimension. AGD is derived only for square loss; no global cross-entropy majorizer, descent proof, or convergence theorem is supplied.

key_findings.claim: Prescription 1 is enforced only at initialization for weights, so the exponential majorizer and convergence constants are not preserved along the actual training trajectory.
key_findings.evidence: The derivation repeatedly uses exact equalities ||W_k||_op = sqrt(d_k/d_{k-1}) to telescope products and bound objectives and gradients. The paper acknowledges drift, gives only a one-step Weyl interval, and neither renormalizes weights nor derives cumulative drift control. The implementation always scales updates using the initial dimensional target rather than the current operator norm.

key_findings.claim: AGD trains the reported fully connected and convolutional systems without tuning its default gain, but the strongest empirical conclusion is viability across selected settings, not superiority to tuned optimizers.
key_findings.evidence: Reported results include 52.7% versus Adam's 53.5% for a depth-16 width-512 CIFAR-10 FCN, 91.2% versus Adam's 92.9% for ResNet-18/CIFAR-10, 67.4% versus Adam's 69.7% for VGG-16/CIFAR-100, and 65.5% ImageNet top-1 for ResNet-50 after 350 epochs. AGD also trains FCNs over widths 64-2048, depths 2-32, and batch sizes 32-4096. These are useful breadth demonstrations, but AGD trails the tuned Adam results quoted in each matched headline comparison.

key_findings.claim: The optimizer comparison is confounded by architecture, initialization, objective, and tuning-budget choices, and it lacks repeated-seed uncertainty.
key_findings.evidence: AGD uses custom semi-orthogonal initialization while Adam and SGD use PyTorch defaults; biases and batch-normalization affine parameters are disabled for everyone because AGD does not support them; most tasks use square loss; learning-rate tuning is a five-value grid without schedules or regularization; and the ImageNet comparator is SGD at fixed 0.1 with no decay. No figure reports seed count, error bars, statistical tests, throughput, gradient-normalization overhead, or matched standard recipes. The paper itself cites a 93.0% tuned CIFAR ResNet recipe versus AGD's 91.2% but does not run it in the controlled comparison.

key_findings.claim: The phrase 'without hyperparameters' means no tuned optimizer learning rate or schedule at gain 1, not a training workflow without choices or optimizer knobs.
key_findings.evidence: Experiments still choose architecture, width, depth, batch size, epochs, loss, augmentation, normalization, initialization family, and unsupported feature removals. Appendix B and the official repository expose a gain hyperparameter, and the discussion says gain or momentum can accelerate convergence; the development repository adds beta and weight-scale multipliers. The paper fairly states that reported runs use gain 1, but the broad title can obscure this narrower scope.

key_findings.claim: The paper and released training code materially diverge from the stated FCN theory.
key_findings.evidence: The theory uses plain ReLU, per-example input norm sqrt(d_0), and square loss ||f-y||^2/(2d_L). The official experiment code multiplies every FCN ReLU output by sqrt(2), uses ordinary channelwise dataset standardization rather than per-example norm enforcement, and computes mean squared error without the 1/2. The sqrt(2)-ReLU is not 1-Lipschitz, so the deep-relative-trust proof as written does not cover that network; doubling the loss also changes G and the automatically selected eta.

anchors.section: A proof of deep relative trust

key_findings.claim: The official artifact is compact and executable at the optimizer level, but it does not support exact reproduction of the published figures and the appendix implementation has a zero-gradient numerical bug.
key_findings.evidence: The current jxbz/agd repository at commit 1f8454d24335d55aeffa1249d34d84d00d37d5d4 provides optimizer, architecture, dataset, and launch code; all Python files compile. It has no pinned environment, tests, seeds, raw logs, checkpoints, plotting code, or figure-data provenance. In the exact Appendix B code, a zero gradient causes division by zero followed by 0*infinity*0 and corrupts weights with NaNs in a direct smoke test. The repository version adds torch.nan_to_num and passes that smoke test, but this fix is absent from the arXiv appendix and unmentioned in the paper.

key_findings.claim: Several exact mathematical presentation defects do not invalidate the main algebra but reduce the reliability of direct reuse.
key_findings.evidence: Fact 1 places right singular vectors of an m-by-n matrix in R^m rather than R^n. The square-loss proof omits the 1/d_L factor from both its cross term and stated gradient even though the lemma statement includes the correct 1/(2d_L) remainder. The cross-entropy proof calls p outer-product p positive definite, although it is rank-one positive semidefinite for multi-class p; the inequality still follows from semidefiniteness.

method.core_idea: Majorize the objective in function space, bound how architecture-scaled weight perturbations move network outputs, and minimize that bound to choose normalized layer updates and a scalar step automatically.
method.mechanism: An exact perturbation identity separates nonlinear model error from the convex loss Bregman divergence. After assuming the model-error inner product vanishes, square loss leaves a quadratic output perturbation. For fully connected ReLU networks, deep relative trust converts layerwise relative operator-norm updates into an exponential output bound. Exact dimensional scaling and rank-one-stable gradients reduce the bound to -eta G + (exp(eta)-1)^2/2; analytic minimization gives eta and normalized gradient updates. A further deep PL assumption supplies a conditional global rate.
assumptions: The dataset-averaged inner product between the output-loss gradient and the model's nonlinear linearization remainder is exactly zero for every selected update.
Every layer gradient has stable rank exactly one, making Frobenius and operator norms equal.
Each input has Euclidean norm sqrt(d_0), each target has norm sqrt(d_L), and every weight matrix retains operator norm sqrt(d_k/d_{k-1}).
The analyzed model is a bias-free feed-forward composition of linear maps and plain 1-Lipschitz ReLUs.
Optimization is full-batch and uses the square objective normalized by 1/(2d_L).
The deep Polyak-Lojasiewicz lower bound holds uniformly with a positive problem-dependent alpha for the global-minimum result.
For cross-entropy, the local Taylor remainder is benign and output perturbations are sufficiently spread across classes.
Per-spatial-submatrix normalization is an adequate heuristic extension from matrices to convolutions.
Residual paths and non-affine batch normalization preserve the useful behavior of the FCN-derived rule despite falling outside the perturbation proof.
A coarse learning-rate sweep and fixed optimizer defaults provide an adequate practical baseline for evaluating automatic learning-rate selection.

techniques.role: Moves composite-objective linearization error into model and loss-output terms.
Represents convex loss curvature in output space for square and cross-entropy losses.
Bounds a deep network's output change from layerwise operator-norm perturbations.
Sets weight and update operator norms using fan-out/fan-in dimensions.
Divides every normalized layer update by network depth.
Aggregates dimension-weighted layer gradient norms into the scalar G.
Chooses eta by closed-form minimization of the exponential upper bound.
Uses each layer gradient's direction while fixing its update norm.
Initializes matrices or convolutional submatrices semi-orthogonally at prescribed scales.
Assumes an architecture-scaled gradient lower bound to turn stationarity into a global rate.

failure_modes: If the nonlinear model remainder aligns with the loss gradient, Assumption 1 fails and the functional expression is not the stated majorizer.
If a minibatch gradient has stable rank above one, normalized-gradient descent is not the exact operator-norm steepest direction used by the theorem.
Weight operator norms drift after initialization, breaking the telescoping prescription and the numerical constants in subsequent descent and convergence arguments.
Cross-entropy steps can leave the local Taylor regime or concentrate on a few logits, invalidating the spread-out perturbation heuristic.
Plain FCN theory does not cover sqrt(2)-scaled ReLUs, convolutional parameter sharing, residual addition, batch normalization, biases, affine parameters, or Transformers.
Stochastic minibatches do not inherit the full-batch majorize-minimize monotonicity proof.
A zero or missing parameter gradient causes division-by-zero or attribute errors in the exact appendix implementation; the current repository fixes only the zero-norm case.
Disabling biases and affine parameters can reduce model quality and makes comparison to standard architectures indirect.
Automatic eta may train reliably yet converge more slowly than a tuned optimizer; the authors report gain and momentum can accelerate it but reintroduce knobs.
Different initialization distributions can make default Adam/SGD failure an initialization-plus-optimizer result rather than an optimizer-only result.
Unregularized square-loss comparisons need not predict standard cross-entropy, weight-decayed, scheduled training performance or generalization.
Absent seeds, logs, dependency pins, and plotting code prevent exact reconstruction of the published curves.
limitations: Author-stated: theory is full-batch while experiments are minibatch, and a stochastic theory remains future work.
Author-stated: derivation covers fully connected networks; convolutions are heuristic, and Transformers, biases, and affine parameters are unsupported.
Author-stated: the work treats optimization rather than generalization or regularization.
Author-stated: gain or momentum can accelerate AGD, and regularization may require at least one hyperparameter.
Reviewer-identified: Assumptions 1 and 2 are exact, update-dependent, unverified, and not empirically audited across layers or time.
Reviewer-identified: the weight-norm prescription required by all key bounds is not maintained beyond initialization.
Reviewer-identified: the global convergence theorem assumes an unproved deep PL constant alpha and therefore does not establish global convergence for the tested networks.
Reviewer-identified: the cross-entropy result is a local expansion with an uncontrolled remainder rather than a global majorization, yet it is used for ImageNet.
Reviewer-identified: experimental FCNs use sqrt(2)-scaled ReLU, standard dataset normalization, and a doubled square-loss convention relative to the derivation.
Reviewer-identified: baseline comparisons use different initialization, coarse learning-rate-only tuning, no competitive schedules or regularization, and no repeated-seed uncertainty.
Reviewer-identified: no compute, throughput, memory peak, gradient-reduction overhead, or tuning-budget-normalized cost is reported.
Reviewer-identified: the exact appendix optimizer has a zero-gradient NaN bug; current repository code fixes it without a versioned release or test.
Reviewer-identified: the repository lacks dependency locks, deterministic seeds, raw metrics, checkpoints, plotting scripts, and automated tests.
Reviewer-identified: the 'without hyperparameters' wording excludes only optimizer rate/schedule tuning at a fixed default gain, not the many training and model choices that remain.
Reviewer-identified: the SVD definition, square-loss proof, and cross-entropy proof contain dimension, missing-factor, and definiteness errors.
open_questions: Can the model-linearization inner product be bounded rather than assumed zero, yielding a valid descent rule with observable slack?
What is the measured stable rank of layer gradients across architectures, batch sizes, training phases, and datasets, and how should AGD change when it exceeds one?
Can current weight operator norms replace fixed initialization scales while retaining an efficient majorizer and preventing cumulative drift?
Is there a global cross-entropy Bregman bound that yields a true automatic step rather than a local spread-out-logit heuristic?
Can the framework derive rules for residual addition, normalization, attention, embeddings, convolutions, biases, and affine parameters compositionally?
What stochastic or high-probability descent guarantee survives minibatch noise without requiring hidden problem constants?
How does AGD compare with D-Adaptation, Prodigy, Mechanic, Schedule-Free methods, modular duality, Muon, and tuned AdamW at matched recipes and tuning compute?
Does automatic architecture scaling improve validation performance and time-to-quality, or mainly stabilize the training objective?
Can gain, momentum, weight decay, and stopping be derived automatically without shifting tunable choices into the loss or architecture?
Which optimizer-free choices such as loss scale, target encoding, data normalization, precision, and batch size change eta enough to undermine invariance claims?
Can a versioned artifact reproduce every figure with pinned software, raw seeds, logs, and hardware-independent smoke tests?
What are the tight impossibility boundaries for a tuning-free optimizer on nonconvex, stochastic, unbounded neural-network objectives?
reusable_insights: Treat architecture as part of the optimizer's geometry rather than flattening every parameter into one Euclidean space.
Separate loss curvature in output space from nonlinear model perturbation before designing a first-order update.
Normalize layer updates in norms matched to the operator semantics of each module.
Distinguish eliminating a learning rate from eliminating schedules, regularization, batch size, stopping, initialization, and loss-scale choices.
Measure every simplifying assumption along the actual trajectory; exact orthogonality and rank-one claims should not remain unaudited.
Recompute or control the state quantities required by a theorem instead of relying on initialization prescriptions after they drift.
Do not call a local Taylor expansion with a signed big-O remainder a global majorizer.
Use identical architectures, initialization, loss, augmentation, and regularization when attributing gains to an optimizer.
Report tuning compute, time-to-quality, memory, communication reductions, and repeated-seed uncertainty alongside final accuracy.
Put numerical guards for zero and missing gradients in normalized-gradient optimizers and test them explicitly.
Cross-check paper equations against the exact loss and activation definitions in training code.
Release raw logs and plotting scripts; rendered curves alone are not a reproducible experiment artifact.

competitive_landscape.title: Training Deep Networks without Learning Rates Through Coin Betting
competitive_landscape.difference: COCOB reduces optimization to coin betting, proves convex and quasi-convex rates, and evaluates a stochastic learning-rate-free optimizer. AGD instead derives architecture-specific relative updates for nonconvex deep compositions, but its guarantees require exact assumptions and do not cover its stochastic experiments.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning-Rate-Free Learning by D-Adaptation
competitive_landscape.difference: D-Adaptation estimates the distance-to-solution scale, has convex Lipschitz guarantees without extra gradient evaluations, wraps SGD and Adam, and reports more than a dozen vision/language tasks. AGD uses network width/depth semantics and no optimizer state, but supports fewer architectures and rests on stronger unmeasured neural assumptions.

competitive_landscape.title: Prodigy: An Expeditiously Adaptive Parameter-Free Learner
competitive_landscape.difference: Prodigy improves D-Adaptation's distance estimate and evaluates logistic regression, CNNs, ViTs, LSTMs, DLRMs, medical reconstruction, RoBERTa, and GPT. It is broadly architecture-agnostic and Adam-compatible; AGD offers an explicit compositional-architecture derivation but much narrower empirical coverage.

competitive_landscape.title: Mechanic: A Learning Rate Tuner
competitive_landscape.difference: Mechanic automatically tunes the scale of any base optimizer and schedule and evaluates large-scale tasks, batch sizes, and optimizer families. It preserves mature optimizer machinery; AGD replaces that machinery with normed architecture-dependent updates and claims lower state memory, at the cost of restricted module support.

competitive_landscape.title: Tuning-Free Stochastic Optimization
competitive_landscape.difference: Khaled et al. formalize tuning-free matching of optimally tuned SGD, prove impossibility on important unbounded convex settings, and give conditional stochastic and nonconvex results. This work places AGD's broad elimination rhetoric in a sharper problem-class and hint-dependent framework that the AGD paper does not address.

competitive_landscape.title: Universal Majorization-Minimization Algorithms
competitive_landscape.difference: Universal MM uses Taylor-mode automatic differentiation to derive majorizers for arbitrary problems automatically and claims convergence from any start without tuning. AGD hand-derives a simpler neural architecture bound and a cheap first-order rule, but only after conditional cancellations and restricted module assumptions.

competitive_landscape.title: Scalable Optimization in the Modular Norm
competitive_landscape.difference: Modular norm recursively assigns natural norms to general neural modules and normalizes any base optimizer for width/depth transfer, with a Modula package. It generalizes AGD's layer-matrix geometry beyond plain FCNs while shifting from complete rate elimination to transferable architecture-aware scaling.

competitive_landscape.title: Modular Duality in Deep Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Modular dualization maps gradients from dual to primal spaces using semantic layer norms and derives GPU-friendly Embed, Linear, and Conv2D updates linked to record-setting NanoGPT training. It develops AGD's architecture-geometry motivation into broader and faster practical optimizers, but does not eliminate all training hyperparameters.

competitive_landscape.title: The Road Less Scheduled
competitive_landscape.difference: Schedule-Free optimization removes dependence on a predetermined stopping horizon by unifying scheduling and iterate averaging, and its AdamW variant won the 2024 AlgoPerf self-tuning track. AGD derives an automatic per-batch scalar and needs no explicit schedule, but lacks comparable self-tuning benchmark evidence and mature AdamW regularization.

competitive_landscape.title: Anytime Training with Schedule-Free Spectral Optimization
competitive_landscape.difference: SF-NorMuon combines schedule-free training with matrix-spectral updates, reports one configuration across multiple language-model scales and 1-8 times Chinchilla horizons, and proves a stationarity guarantee. It operationalizes both norm-aware updates and horizon robustness on Transformers, two directions left open by AGD, while retaining a fixed hyperparameter configuration rather than claiming none.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Functional majorization plus neural architectural perturbation bounds yields a rigorous, first-order, architecture-dependent optimizer that automatically supplies learning-rate scale, width/depth scaling, and schedule without hyperparameters.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper contributes a clean perturbation decomposition, an FCN-specific exponential bound, the closed-form AGD rule, conditional stationarity/global rates, and breadth experiments through ResNet-50/ImageNet. Relative updates, deep relative trust, operator scaling, muP width scaling, majorize-minimize, Bregman geometry, gradient normalization, and learning-rate-free optimization all predate it; D-Adaptation is a stronger concurrent parameter-free baseline that is not compared.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The novel synthesis is architecture-aware analytic step selection: AGD connects output-space loss geometry to operator-norm perturbation bounds and produces an unusually simple state-free rule. The 'rigorous' and 'without hyperparameters' framing is substantially narrower than the title because the proof assumes exact orthogonality, rank-one-stable gradients, persistent norm equalities, full batches, square loss, and plain bias-free FCNs, while the experiments and code violate several of those conditions. Later modular-norm/duality work is the more durable continuation of its architecture-geometry idea; D-Adaptation, Prodigy, Mechanic, and Schedule-Free methods are stronger practical comparators for automatic rate or schedule selection.

reviewer_notes: Read all 23 pages of the exact arXiv v1 artifact, including every definition, prescription, assumption, proposition, lemma, corollary, theorem, displayed derivation, Algorithm 1, Tables 1-2, Figures 1-7, references, Appendix A proofs, and Appendix B implementation. Rendered and visually inspected every page and reconciled all plot captions and embedded figure assets against the LaTeX source. The cached PDF is byte-identical to the current arXiv PDF on 2026-08-24; the official source archive SHA-256 is 706c7c7cf5c287a5263a5c2b40f02510044cba9abc6dfb4b01a3b4b91feebdfe. Audited official repository jxbz/agd at commit 1f8454d24335d55aeffa1249d34d84d00d37d5d4 (latest commit 2023-06-25) and the explicitly labeled development repository C1510/agd_exp at 61fb6f7347192deb98b005f0a382c57b60460f96 (2023-07-30). All Python files compile. A CPU smoke test verified that the exact arXiv Appendix B code produces non-finite weights on an exactly zero gradient, whereas the later official repository's torch.nan_to_num guard leaves them finite and unchanged. No dataset download or full training reproduction was attempted because exact dependencies, seeds, raw metrics, checkpoints, hardware, and plotting inputs are absent. The root README claims CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 for the code but the repository has no root LICENSE file; the TMLR template license bundled under latex is not an experiment-code license file. Competitor titles, abstracts, mechanisms, and current official arXiv versions were checked through 2026-08-24.
